title: GitHub Basics for Beginners: A Complete Step-by-Step Guide for Students
meta_title: GitHub Basics for Beginners: Git, Repositories, Commits, Branches and Pull Requests Explained
meta_description: Learn GitHub from scratch: what Git and GitHub are, how to create a repository, commit code, use branches, make pull requests and build a strong student profile.
author: naacollege.in Editorial Team
excerpt: GitHub is the place where developers store, share and collaborate on code. This beginner guide explains Git and GitHub in simple language with practical commands and examples.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: If you want a career in software, data science, AI or even cybersecurity, you will hear about GitHub very soon. Recruiters check GitHub profiles, open source projects live there, and almost every tech team uses it to manage code.
This guide explains everything a beginner needs: what Git and GitHub are, how to install and set up, the most useful commands, branching, pull requests and tips to build a profile that impresses.

sections.heading: Git vs GitHub: What Is the Difference?
paragraphs: Git is a version control system. It runs on your computer and tracks every change you make to your files, so you can go back to an older version, compare changes and work safely.

GitHub is a website and platform that hosts Git repositories online. It adds collaboration features such as pull requests, issues, project boards and automation. Other similar platforms are GitLab and Bitbucket, but GitHub is the most popular.
sections.takeaway: Git is the tool. GitHub is the online home for your Git projects.

sections.heading: Why Should Students Learn GitHub?
list: Keeps a backup of your projects online
Shows your skills through a public portfolio
Lets you collaborate with classmates without overwriting each other's work
Is required knowledge for internships and developer jobs
Gives you a way to contribute to open source projects
Helps you track mistakes and undo them safely

sections.heading: Step 1: Create a GitHub Account
paragraphs: Go to github.com and sign up with your email. Choose a professional username because it becomes part of your profile link. Something like your name works better than a random nickname. Add a clear profile photo and a short bio.
Enable two-factor authentication in your security settings to protect your account.

sections.heading: Step 2: Install Git
paragraphs: Download Git from the official Git website and install it. On Windows it comes with Git Bash. On macOS and Linux you can install it using the package manager. After installing, open a terminal and check the version.

sections.heading: Step 3: Configure Git
paragraphs: Tell Git who you are. This information is attached to every commit you make. Use the same email as your GitHub account.
sections.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

sections.heading: Step 4: Create Your First Repository
paragraphs: You can start locally and then connect to GitHub. Create a folder, initialise Git, add a file, and make your first commit.
sections.code:
mkdir my-first-project
cd my-first-project
git init
echo "# My First Project" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"

sections.heading: Step 5: Connect to GitHub and Push
paragraphs: On GitHub, click New repository, give it a name and create it without adding files. GitHub will show you a repository URL. Link your local project to it and push your code.
sections.code:
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/my-first-project.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
sections.note: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations over HTTPS. Use a personal access token, GitHub CLI login, the GitHub Desktop app, or set up SSH keys.

sections.heading: The Everyday Git Workflow
paragraphs: Most of your daily work follows a simple loop: check status, stage changes, commit and push.
sections.code:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Describe what you changed"
git push
paragraphs_after: Write commit messages that explain what changed and why, for example Fix login button alignment. Avoid messages like final or changes2.

sections.heading: Branches: Work Safely Without Breaking Your Project
paragraphs: A branch lets you build a new feature without touching your stable code. The main branch usually holds the working version. You create a new branch for each feature or fix, then merge it when it is ready.
sections.code:
git switch -c add-login-page
# make changes
git add .
git commit -m "Add login page"
git push -u origin add-login-page

sections.heading: Pull Requests: How Teams Collaborate
paragraphs: After pushing a branch, open GitHub and click Compare and pull request. Write a clear title and description, then submit. Teammates can review your code, leave comments and approve it. When everyone is happy, the PR is merged into the main branch.
Pull requests are also how you contribute to open source: fork the project, create a branch, make your change, push it, and open a pull request to the original repository.

sections.heading: Handling Merge Conflicts
paragraphs: A merge conflict happens when two people change the same lines of a file. Git cannot decide which version to keep, so it asks you. Open the file, look for the conflict markers, choose the correct content, remove the markers, then stage and commit the result.
Do not panic. Conflicts are normal in team projects. Pull often and keep branches small to reduce them.

sections.heading: Important Files in a Repository
list: README.md: explains what the project does, how to install it and how to use it
.gitignore: lists files Git should not track, such as passwords, environment files and build folders
LICENSE: tells others how they can use your code
requirements.txt or package.json: lists dependencies
sections.note: Never upload API keys, passwords or private data to a public repository. If you do by mistake, revoke the key immediately.

sections.heading: Other Useful GitHub Features
list: Issues: track bugs and tasks
Projects: kanban-style boards for planning
GitHub Pages: host a free static website or portfolio from a repository
GitHub Actions: automate tests and deployments
Codespaces: write code in a cloud development environment
Discussions and stars: community interaction and bookmarking projects
Copilot: AI coding assistant available through GitHub with its own plans

sections.heading: How to Build a Strong GitHub Profile as a Student
list: Create a profile README that introduces you, your skills and your best projects
Pin your best six repositories
Add clear README files with screenshots and setup steps to every project
Commit regularly instead of uploading everything on one day
Build real projects: a portfolio site, a to-do app, a data analysis notebook, a small game
Contribute to beginner-friendly open source issues labelled good first issue
Keep repository names meaningful and your code tidy

sections.heading: Common Beginner Mistakes
list: Committing sensitive files such as passwords and keys
Writing meaningless commit messages
Working directly on main in team projects
Forgetting to pull before pushing
Uploading huge files or entire node_modules folders
Using GitHub only as storage without documentation

faq.question: Is GitHub free?
faq.answer: Yes. GitHub offers free accounts with public and private repositories. Paid plans add extra features for teams and organisations.

faq.question: Do I need to know coding before learning Git?
faq.answer: Basic coding helps, but you can learn Git using simple text files. It works with any kind of file.

faq.question: Is Git the same as GitHub?
faq.answer: No. Git is the version control tool. GitHub is the online platform that hosts Git repositories.

faq.question: Can I use GitHub without the command line?
faq.answer: Yes. GitHub Desktop and the web interface let you do many tasks visually, though learning basic commands is very valuable.

faq.question: Does GitHub help in getting a job?
faq.answer: A well-maintained profile with real projects shows practical skills and consistency, which many recruiters appreciate.

conclusion: GitHub may feel confusing on day one, but a few commands and habits take you a long way. Start with one small project, commit regularly, write clear READMEs and slowly explore branches and pull requests. In a few weeks you will have a profile that proves your skills.
disclaimer: Interface layouts and authentication methods on GitHub can change. Check the official GitHub Docs for the latest instructions.
